newsitem.title: USA: U.S. sees no sign of Chinese troops in Kinshasa.
newsitem.headline: U.S. sees no sign of Chinese troops in Kinshasa.

text.p: The United States on Tuesday ridiculed allegations by Zairean rebels that hundreds of Chinese troops had arrived in Kinshasa to help repulse a feared rebel attack.
"That seems like a fantastically improbable story," State Department spokesman Nicholas Burns said. "We see no evidence of that whatsoever."

Rebel "finance minister" Mawana Nanga Mawampanga said in the southern city of Lubumbashi that 400 Chinese troops were in Kinshasa. The Zairean government of President Mobutu Sese Seko and China have both denied the allegation.
It was the second rebel claim that U.S. officials have denied in recent days. Last week they dismissed allegations that Mobutu's government was planning to massacre expatriates living in Kinshasa.
Burns described the situation in Zaire as "quite worrisome" and said every effort should be made to arrange a meeting between Mobutu and rebel leader Laurent Kabila.
Mobutu's son said Monday that his father, who has been suffering from prostate cancer, would not be able to attend a planned meeting this week in Cape Town, South Africa.

"We hope very much that it might still be possible for a meeting to be arranged," Burns said. "If health is a problem, then perhaps another location can be worked out that would be more convenient for President Mobutu."

"Without a meeting, there's very little prospect, we think, of a ceasefire or agreements on any kind of transitional political arrangements that would lead Zaire out of chaos, away from civil war," he added.
Burns also expressed renewed concern about the plight of some 80,000 to 100,000 Rwandan refugees stranded in eastern Zaire, whose planned repatriation by air has been delayed.

He said the United States backed a call by U.N. High Commissioner for Refugees Sadako Ogata for the rebels to allow aid workers to resume relief operations among the refugees, and to let the airlift begin.
